raw_case_text:
A 63-year-old male complained of rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms in the spring for the previous 10 years, together with pruritus of the roof of the mouth and the ears following the consumption of drupes, nuts, apples, and carrots. Treatment of these symptoms with oral antihistamines, nasal GCs, and antihistamine eye drops was only partially effective. The patient was reportedly sensitized to tree, weed and grass pollen, but had no symptoms during weed and grass pollination season. The patient was HIV-positive and had been refused AIT for many years. When the patient consulted in our institution, he underwent a comprehensive allergologic and immunologic work-up. Total IgE was 375 IU/ml. The Immunocap assay confirmed sensitization to tree 74.9 IU/ml (5 class), weed 18.6 IU/ml (4 class) and grass pollen 14.3 IU/ml (3 class). The patient was diagnosed with severe intermittent allergic rhinoconjunctivitis, he had been receiving active HART for 8 years, and the disease progression had been monitored by an infectious disease specialist.
In view of the incomplete symptom control with pharmacologic therapy and the absence of signs of viral replication or clinically significant changes in lymphocyte subsets (i.e. a CD4+ count within the normal range), we recommended birch pollen sublingual AIT. After the patient had given his written, informed consent, he underwent two courses of pre- and co-seasonal therapy Staloral  Birch from Stallergenes (Antony, France); daily maintenance dose: 300 IR) from December to May. CD4+ cell counts and PCR tests for the HIV load were performed at 3-month intervals during the first year of treatment, and then at 6-month intervals during the second year. As in case #1, no positive PCR results and no negative trends in the CD4+ cell count were observed at any time during treatment and follow-up.
During the treatment period, the patient experienced the local adverse reactions commonly associated with sublingual AIT (pronounced pruritus and moderate edema in the sublingual region starting 1 or 2 minutes after administration and persisting for 25 minutes). However, the symptoms were managed with antihistamines and did not modify require modification of the AIT regimen. No systemic reactions were reported.
Based on the patient diary, an improvement was noted following the first course of pre- and co-seasonal AIT: mild rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms were successfully managed with standard doses of oral antihistamine, and the patient did not require topical GCs or topical antihistamines. Following the second course of AIT, the patient noted a further reduction in the severity and duration of rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms, which were fully controlled with oral antihistamines. The patient was advised to continue AIT, to monitor the viral load and CD4+ cell count, and to keep a diary of symptoms and concomitant medications (Table 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 63-year-old male presenting with a 10-year history of springtime rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms and oral pruritus upon eating drupes, nuts, apples, and carrots.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 10-year history of recurring springtime rhinoconjunctivitis, along with itching of the palate and ears provoked by the consumption of drupes, nuts, apples, and carrots. Prior pharmacotherapy with oral antihistamines, intranasal glucocorticoids, and antihistamine ophthalmic drops yielded only partial symptom relief. Allergen immunotherapy had previously been withheld for many years. He experienced local adverse reactions to sublingual therapy consisting of pronounced sublingual pruritus and moderate edema onsetting within 1-2 minutes and lasting 25 minutes, which responded to antihistamines without systemic reactions.
subjective.past_medical_history: Underlying chronic viral infection on active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) for 8 years, monitored regularly by an infectious disease specialist; known sensitization to tree, weed, and grass pollens.
subjective.review_of_systems: Pruritus of the roof of the mouth and ears following ingestion of stone fruits, nuts, apples, and carrots; denies rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms during weed and grass pollination seasons.

objective.physical_examination: Localized examination following sublingual therapy demonstrated pronounced pruritus and moderate edema in the sublingual region lasting 25 minutes; no systemic adverse reactions observed.
objective.routine_investigations: Total IgE: 375 IU/ml. ImmunoCAP specific IgE assay: Sensitization to tree pollen 74.9 IU/ml (class 5), weed pollen 18.6 IU/ml (class 4), and grass pollen 14.3 IU/ml (class 3).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Severe intermittent allergic rhinoconjunctivitis with pollen-food allergy syndrome in a patient with well-controlled human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection on antiretroviral therapy (HAART). HIV monitoring: CD4+ T-cell count remained within normal range and HIV RNA PCR demonstrated no viral replication or negative CD4+ trends at 3-month intervals during year 1 and 6-month intervals during year 2 of treatment. Plan & Outcome: Initiated on birch pollen sublingual allergen immunotherapy (SLIT; Staloral Birch, daily maintenance dose 300 IR) administered pre- and co-seasonally from December to May across two courses. Local sublingual edema and pruritus were managed with oral antihistamines. Following two courses, rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms markedly decreased and were fully controlled with oral antihistamines alone, eliminating the need for topical corticosteroids or topical antihistamines. Advised to continue SLIT and longitudinal monitoring.
